Because the framework header is Objective-C, and Objective-C has no closed hierarchies — a sealed type arrives as an ordinary open class with subclasses, so Swift has no way to know the list is complete.

### What the header actually contains
- `sealed interface AuthState` becomes `@interface SharedAuthState`, and every subtype becomes a subclass whose name is flattened onto the parent's: `AuthState.LoggedIn` is `SharedAuthStateLoggedIn`.
- `data object Anonymous` becomes a class with a `+shared` singleton accessor, so recognising it in Swift is an `is` check against that class.
- Nothing marks the class as closed. The Swift `switch` degrades into a chain of `case let x as ...` casts, and the compiler requires `default` because someone could always subclass.

### Why that costs more than ugliness
Add a fourth subtype in Kotlin and the Android `when` stops compiling — the iOS build does not. The new state falls into `default` and ships as "nothing happened". Exhaustiveness is a Kotlin-side guarantee that does not survive the bridge, and no amount of code review replaces it.

Two ways to get it back:
- **SKIE** regenerates the hierarchy as a real Swift enum, and `switch onEnum(of: state)` is checked by the Swift compiler.
- Export a `fold`-shaped function instead of the type: one Kotlin function taking a lambda per case. Kotlin enforces coverage, and adding a case adds a parameter, so every Swift call site breaks.

The model: make the compiler that knows the hierarchy enforce it. Either generate the Swift enum, or don't export the hierarchy — export the function that consumes it.

Objective-C has lightweight generics on classes and nothing else, so Kotlin's class-level type parameters survive as compile-time hints and every other use of a generic degrades to `Any`.

### What crosses and what does not
- **Generic classes** export as Objective-C lightweight generics: `class Page<T>` gives Swift `Page<Post>`. Lightweight generics are erased at runtime, so this is a promise to the Swift compiler and nothing more.
- **Generic interfaces do not.** An Objective-C protocol cannot take a type parameter, so `interface Repository<T>` loses it and every method returns `Any?`. That one rule is why so much exported KMP code is an abstract class rather than an interface.
- **Generic functions do not.** A type parameter on a function has nowhere to live in a selector, so `fun <T> List<T>.secondOrNull(): T?` hands Swift `Any?`.
- **Primitives box.** `Page<Int>.items` is `[KotlinInt]` in Swift, and you unwrap `.int32Value` by hand.

### Where it actually bites
`sealed class Result<out T>` is the worst combination on the bridge: non-exhaustive because Objective-C has no closed hierarchies, and untyped because the payload sits in a generic position. The Swift call site casts twice — once to find the case, once to read the value — and neither cast is checked.

What to do: export concrete types. `FeedResult` and `UserResult` with a typed payload per case are boring, and the Swift compiler can check them. Keep the generic machinery in `commonMain` and let the exported surface be its un-generic edge — the same discipline you would apply to any public API, except the type system on the other side is far weaker than yours.

Objective-C has neither default arguments nor overloading, so the header generator drops the defaults outright and mangles any name that would collide.

### Defaults
`fun search(query: String, limit: Int = 20, offset: Int = 0)` produces exactly one selector, `searchQuery:limit:offset:`, and Swift has to pass all three. `@JvmOverloads` is a JVM annotation and does nothing on Native. Your options are to declare the convenience overloads by hand, or let **SKIE** generate real Swift default values.

### Names
- A selector is the function name plus the parameter names, so `load(id: Long)` becomes `loadId:`. Two overloads differing only in parameter *type* collide, and the compiler disambiguates by appending an underscore — Swift gets `load(id:)` and `load(id_:)`, and which is which follows declaration order.
- Anything clashing with `NSObject` is renamed: a data class's `copy()` becomes `doCopy()`, `toString()` becomes `description`, `equals()` becomes `isEqual:`, `hashCode` becomes `hash`.
- Packages are flattened into one namespace prefixed by the framework's `baseName`, so two `User` classes in different packages collide and one gets a suffix.
- A Kotlin `object` exposes `+shared`, a `companion object` exposes `+companion`, and top-level declarations land on a class named after the file, `SharedSearchKt`.

The tools: `@ObjCName(swiftName = "...")` renames a declaration for Swift without touching Kotlin call sites, and `@HiddenFromObjC` keeps one out of the header entirely. Both are opt-in experimental annotations.

The rule of thumb: the exported surface is a separate API, not a projection of your Kotlin. Give it distinct names and no overloads and the mangler never fires.

Because the generated bridge is a one-way completion handler: Swift hands Kotlin a block and gets back nothing that could carry a cancel.

### What the compiler generates
`suspend fun fetchUser(id: Long): User` becomes an Objective-C method taking a `completionHandler:` block with a value and an `NSError`, which Swift imports as `func fetchUser(id: Int64) async throws -> User`. It reads like structured concurrency and is not: the coroutine is started in a scope the bridge owns, and the only channel between the runtimes is that block being invoked once. `Task.cancel()` marks the Swift task; nothing on the Kotlin side is listening, so the request runs to completion and the result is discarded.

The same signature carries a second surprise. An exported suspend function may only be called from the main thread by default; calling one off the main thread traps. The binary option `objcExportSuspendFunctionLaunchThreadRestriction=none` lifts it when you are sure the code is thread-safe.

### Getting cancellation back
- **SKIE** and **KMP-NativeCoroutines** both wrap the export so cancelling the Swift `Task` cancels the Kotlin `Job`. This is why most teams add one of them in week one.
- By hand: don't export the suspend function. Export a launcher that returns a cancellable handle, and let Swift cancel it in `onDisappear` or `deinit`.

Rule of thumb: a raw exported `suspend` is fire-and-forget wearing `async` syntax. If the work is expensive or the screen can vanish, the handle has to be part of the API.

A raw `Flow` crosses as an opaque Objective-C class whose only member is `collect(collector:completionHandler:)`, and `FlowCollector` is a generic interface — so Swift would have to implement a protocol just to receive `Any?` values one at a time.

### The three real options
- **Hand-rolled wrapper.** A Kotlin class that takes a `(T) -> Unit`, calls `launchIn` on a scope you own, and returns a cancellable handle. No dependencies, exact types, and you write one per stream — fine for three flows, tedious for thirty. Swift gets a callback, not something it can `await`.
- **KMP-NativeCoroutines.** A KSP plugin: annotate with `@NativeCoroutines` (`@NativeCoroutinesState` for a `StateFlow`) and it generates a `…Native` member per declaration. Its Swift package then gives you `asyncSequence(for:)`, a Combine `Publisher` via `createPublisher(for:)`, and async/await — all with cancellation wired through. Costs a KSP step, an annotation on every exported declaration, and a Swift dependency in the iOS project.
- **SKIE.** A compiler plugin that rewrites the framework: `Flow<T>` becomes `SkieSwiftFlow<T>`, which *is* an `AsyncSequence`, so `for await posts in repo.posts()` compiles with no annotations at all, and sealed classes, enums and default arguments improve in the same pass.

### Choosing
SKIE if the team accepts a compiler plugin pinned to your Kotlin version; KMP-NativeCoroutines if you need Combine publishers or want the bridged surface to be explicit and reviewable; hand-rolled only when the exported surface is genuinely small.

Whatever you pick, cancellation decides it. A stream Swift cannot stop is a subscription held by a Kotlin scope and a closure held by ARC — a leak neither collector can see.

SKIE is a Kotlin compiler plugin from Touchlab that generates a Swift layer on top of the Objective-C framework and ships it inside the same framework, so the iOS project installs nothing and imports nothing new.

### What it generates
- Kotlin `enum class` and sealed hierarchies become real Swift enums. `switch onEnum(of: state)` is exhaustive and rejects a `default` you don't need.
- `Flow`, `StateFlow` and `SharedFlow` become `SkieSwiftFlow` and friends, conforming to `AsyncSequence`.
- `suspend` functions become Swift `async` with Swift task cancellation propagated into the Kotlin `Job` — the one thing the plain bridge cannot do at all.
- Default arguments become real Swift default parameter values, so one Kotlin declaration is one Swift function again.

### What it costs
- **Build time.** Every framework link now also compiles generated Swift, and on a wide exported API that is the slowest step of the iOS build. The `skie { features { … } }` block turns individual features off, per module or per declaration, when it matters.
- **Version coupling.** SKIE releases track Kotlin releases, so a Kotlin upgrade waits for a matching SKIE.
- **A layer in the debugger.** Stepping from Swift into Kotlin passes through generated files, and crash stacks carry SKIE frames.

What it does not fix: it is still Objective-C underneath. Generics still erase, nullability is still a promise rather than a check, and name mangling still happens.

The honest pitch to that lead: SKIE buys compiler-checked exhaustiveness and real cancellation on the Swift side. Those are the two guarantees the bridge destroys and the two you cannot restore with discipline.

Only exceptions listed in `@Throws` are converted to `NSError`; every other Kotlin exception reaching Objective-C is treated as unhandled and terminates the process, and no Swift `catch` can intercept it.

### The mechanism
- `@Throws(MyError::class)` adds an `NSError **` out-parameter to the selector, which Swift imports as `throws`. At runtime a matching exception arrives as an `NSError` with domain `KotlinException`, and the original `Throwable` sits in `userInfo` under the `KotlinException` key — cast it back if you need the Kotlin type.
- Anything not listed goes through Kotlin/Native's unhandled-exception path: an immediate crash whose report shows Kotlin/Native frames and no Swift ones, which is why these look like SDK bugs in the crash dashboard.
- Suspend functions get the error slot for free — Swift sees `async throws` — but the same rule decides *which* exceptions travel through it. An unannotated suspend function that throws still terminates.
- `@Throws(Exception::class)` stops the crashes and gives Swift one untyped `NSError`. The type you actually needed is only reachable through `userInfo`.

### What to do instead
Don't throw across the boundary. Catch inside the shared module and return a sealed result naming the cases the UI must handle — `Ok`, `Offline`, `Unauthorized` — which also hands Swift something it can switch on. Keep `@Throws` for the one or two calls where a Swift `try` genuinely reads better.

The reverse direction has its own switch: an `NSException` raised in Objective-C code that Kotlin calls also terminates, unless the framework is built with `-Xbinary=foreignExceptionMode=objc-wrap`, which turns it into a catchable `ForeignException`.

Mental model: the bridge carries values, not control flow.

Because nullability in the generated header is a promise to the Swift compiler, not a runtime check — Kotlin/Native does not re-validate arguments at the boundary, so any nil Swift was not forced to unwrap walks straight into a non-null Kotlin parameter.

### Where Swift stops helping
- The header wraps declarations in `NS_ASSUME_NONNULL_BEGIN` and marks Kotlin's nullable types `_Nullable`, so ordinary call sites really are checked. That is the part that works.
- Anything the header leaves unannotated, Swift imports as an implicitly unwrapped optional — `String!`, usable without unwrapping, nil at first touch. Hand-written Objective-C, cinterop headers nobody audited, and values that reached Swift through a generic position or `Any` all land here.
- Generic positions erase to `Any?`, so a value pulled out of an exported generic container is an optional the Swift compiler cannot connect back to Kotlin's declared type.

### The three ways it lands
1. **Deep inside Kotlin, far from the call site.** The nil is stored in a non-null field and fails at the first real use; the crash report is a Kotlin/Native stack with no Swift frames to blame.
2. **As a process kill, not an error.** `lateinit` read before initialisation and `!!` on a null both throw exceptions that appear in nobody's `@Throws` list, so they terminate rather than surface.
3. **On the way in.** Kotlin calling an unannotated Objective-C API gets a platform type `T!` with no compiler check; store that in a non-null property and Kotlin now hands Swift a "non-null" that is nil.

Treat every exported entry point as untrusted input: nullable parameters validated once at the edge, no `lateinit` and no `!!` in exported code, unaudited ObjC APIs wrapped in a thin Kotlin layer that types them nullable. The header documents your intent; only your own code enforces it.

Either the iOS build compiles Kotlin itself or it consumes a versioned binary, and that choice — not the packaging format — is what the iOS team feels every day.

### Direct integration, one repo
- A Run Script phase calls `./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode`; Gradle builds the framework for the current architecture and configuration and drops it into the app bundle.
- Every Mac and every CI runner then needs a JDK and a warm Gradle cache, and a cold shared build lands on top of an ordinary iOS build.
- Xcode 15+ defaults `ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING` to `YES`, which makes that script fail outright. Turn it off, and declare the phase's input and output files so it is skipped when nothing changed.

### A published XCFramework, two repos
- `XCFramework()` in the Gradle DSL gives you `assembleSharedXCFramework` — one artifact holding the device and simulator slices.
- SPM consumes it as a `.binaryTarget`: a local `path` while you iterate, `url` plus `checksum` for a released one. The iOS build never runs Gradle.
- The price is a release loop — bump, publish, resolve. Touchlab's KMMBridge automates build, upload, checksum and tag if you would rather not write it.

### The CocoaPods plugin
- `kotlin("native.cocoapods")` generates a podspec, so `pod install` drives the Kotlin build. It also gives Kotlin `pod(...)` cinterop, still the easiest way to call a Pod-only SDK from shared code.
- Against it: Ruby and CocoaPods back in the toolchain of a team that has moved to SPM, and CocoaPods itself is in maintenance mode.

Rule of thumb: monorepo and one team, direct integration; separate iOS repo or an SDK you ship to others, publish an XCFramework and consume it through SPM. Keep the CocoaPods plugin only when Kotlin needs to consume Pods.

`isStatic = true` links the Kotlin binary into whatever consumes it at build time, dynamic ships a separate `.framework` that dyld loads at launch — and with several targets in one app that difference is not only launch time, it is how many Kotlin runtimes you are running.

### What each one does
- Static: the linker pulls Kotlin into the app binary. Nothing to embed or sign, no extra image for dyld, and unreferenced Kotlin code can be stripped — though everything exported to Objective-C is kept alive by its metadata, so the win is over your internals.
- Dynamic: one more image to map, rebind and register Objective-C classes for at every launch, plus an embed-and-sign step. One framework is milliseconds rather than a stall; a habit of many frameworks is what shows up in a launch trace.

### The extension trap
- A static framework is linked into every target that uses it. The app and the widget each get a private copy: the bytes are duplicated, and so is the Kotlin runtime — two heaps, two collectors, two sets of top-level state. A shared `object SessionStore` becomes two objects that never see each other's writes.
- A dynamic framework is embedded once in the app bundle and loaded by both, so code and state are genuinely shared.

### Crash reports
- Dynamic produces `Shared.framework.dSYM` next to the framework. It is a separate file and a separate upload, and forgetting it is why Kotlin frames come back as hex addresses.
- Static folds the Kotlin symbols into the app's own dSYM, so the upload you already have covers them.

Rule of thumb: a single consumer, go static and enjoy simpler symbols and one less image at launch; app plus extensions, or anything that must share state across targets, go dynamic. Set `isStatic` deliberately instead of inheriting whatever the template picked.

Each Kotlin/Native framework is a self-contained program: it embeds the stdlib, the runtime, the garbage collector and every klib it links, so two frameworks mean two Kotlin runtimes that cannot see each other.

### What you actually see
- The framework's `baseName` is the prefix on every exported class, so two frameworks both named `Shared` export `SharedBase`, `SharedKotlinInt` and friends twice. The Objective-C runtime logs "Class SharedBase is implemented in both …; one of the two will be used", and which one is undefined.
- With static frameworks the same collision arrives earlier and louder, as duplicate symbols at link time.
- Give them distinct base names and the clash goes away — but `SdkInstant` and `SharedInstant` are now different Objective-C classes over the same Kotlin type. Handing one to the other does not compile, and a cast at the seam fails at runtime.
- The binary carries two stdlibs, and each runtime has its own heap, its own collector and its own top-level state.

### The way out
- One Kotlin binary per app. Build an umbrella module that depends on everything shared and `export()`s the libraries whose types appear in the API — `export` only works on an `api` dependency, never `implementation`.
- For a vendor SDK, ask for the klib published to Maven instead of a pre-built framework; it then links into your framework and there is one runtime again.
- If they will not, isolate them: unique base names, and no Kotlin object ever crosses from one framework to the other. Strings, numbers and Swift structs at that boundary only.

Mental model: a Kotlin/Native framework is a statically linked runtime wearing a framework's clothes, not a library you can compose with another one.

LLDB can stop inside Kotlin because the Kotlin/Native compiler emits DWARF, but only for a debug-configuration framework whose recorded source paths still exist on the machine you are debugging from.

### Why the breakpoint does not hit
- The framework has to be the debug variant. With direct integration the Run Script derives it from Xcode's `CONFIGURATION`, and `KOTLIN_FRAMEWORK_BUILD_TYPE` overrides that — pinned to `release`, there are no line tables and nothing to stop on.
- A pre-built XCFramework downloaded from CI records the build agent's absolute paths. Your local `.kt` sits at a different path, so LLDB has the symbol but not the source; `settings set target.source-map` is the fix, and this is the real day-to-day cost of the binary-artifact setup.
- Kotlin frames are mangled — `kfun:com.app.FeedRepo#load(){}`. Symbolic breakpoints and `bt` work fine once you type the mangled name.

### Making values readable
- Out of the box the variables pane shows Kotlin objects as untyped Objective-C instances. Touchlab's `xcode-kotlin` installs LLDB formatters and Kotlin highlighting, and is the difference between debugging and printing.
- The other half of the answer is not to debug Kotlin in Xcode at all: Android Studio or IntelliJ with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin launches and attaches to the iOS app, with real Kotlin breakpoints, watches and stepping.

### On the seam
- An exception that escapes Kotlin into Objective-C terminates the process, and the top frames are Kotlin runtime frames — scroll down to the `kfun:` frames for your own code.
- Keep the framework's `.dSYM`; without it a release crash symbolicates to hex and no amount of local debugging will help.

Rule of thumb: Swift bugs in Xcode, Kotlin bugs in the Kotlin IDE, and a mixed session only when the bug lives exactly on the boundary.
code_example:
# Xcode > Build Phases > Run Script. The framework variant is what decides
# whether you can debug at all — the task reads Xcode's CONFIGURATION.
cd "$SRCROOT/.."
./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode
#   export KOTLIN_FRAMEWORK_BUILD_TYPE=release   <- pinning this in a Debug
#   scheme is the usual reason breakpoints silently stop working

# Readable Kotlin values in the Xcode variables pane (LLDB formatters)
brew install touchlab/kotlin/xcode-kotlin
xcode-kotlin install     # drops the formatters into ~/.lldbinit for every Xcode

# Stop on a Kotlin function by its mangled name
(lldb) breakpoint set --name 'kfun:com.app.FeedRepo#load(){}'
(lldb) bt                # Swift frames and kfun: frames in one stack

# Framework built on CI, sources checked out locally: remap the paths
(lldb) settings set target.source-map /Users/ci/agent/work/shared /Users/me/proj/shared

# Release crashes: the dSYM lives next to the framework, not inside the app
xcrun dwarfdump --uuid \
  shared/build/bin/iosArm64/releaseFramework/Shared.framework.dSYM

Most "leaks" at this boundary are not ARC cycles at all: a running coroutine is a Kotlin GC root, so a ViewModel with a live collector stays alive no matter what Swift does or does not retain.

### The three shapes, in the order to check them
1. **A live job.** `flow.onEach { … }.launchIn(scope)` roots the collector, the collector holds your lambda, the lambda holds the Swift block. Nothing on the Swift side retains anything, so Instruments' Leaks and the memory graph are both clean — and only cancelling the scope frees it.
2. **A real cross-runtime cycle.** ARC retains the Objective-C wrapper of a Kotlin object, which makes that object a GC root; the Kotlin object holds a Swift closure that captures the Swift owner. Neither collector sees the whole loop. `[weak self]` fixes it only when `self` is the object on the loop — capturing a coordinator that owns the view keeps the loop closed.
3. **No leak at all.** Dropping the last Swift reference does not free Kotlin memory; it unregisters a root, and the object dies at the next collection. Footprint staying flat for a while is expected.

### Proving it instead of guessing
- Count `init` and `close` in the Kotlin class and log both. Two inits and no close is a lifetime bug whatever Instruments says.
- Force a collection with `kotlin.native.runtime.GC.collect()` before you measure, and build the debug framework with `-Xruntime-logs=gc=info` to watch the collector actually run.
- Xcode's memory graph still answers the Swift half: if nothing there retains the wrapper, the retainer is Kotlin.

Rule: every subscription hands back a cancellation handle, and whoever started it cancels it. The shared module never owns a screen's scope.

Kotlin/Native stopped enforcing anything years ago — freezing, `freeze()`, `@SharedImmutable` and `InvalidMutabilityException` are gone and objects are shared across threads as on the JVM — so every rule left at this boundary is Apple's, and placing the main-thread hop is your job.

### Still main-thread only
- Everything UIKit and SwiftUI. `objectWillChange` and `@Published` must fire on the main thread or you get "Publishing changes from background threads is not allowed" and, eventually, torn view state.
- Put the hop somewhere visible: `flowOn` or `withContext(Dispatchers.Main)` in Kotlin, or `await MainActor.run` in Swift. What you cannot do is assume the flow arrives on main because it usually did.
- `Dispatchers.Main` on iOS needs a run loop, so a shared test that touches it fails unless the dispatcher is injected. And `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` is unsupported on Native — it throws, which surprises everyone who copied the pattern from the Android side.

### No longer forbidden, still your problem
- Shared mutable state compiles and races exactly as it does on the JVM. Use `Mutex`, confine writes to one dispatcher, or keep state in a `StateFlow` written from a single place.
- `@ThreadLocal` remains for genuinely per-thread state; a top-level `val` is initialized on first access and then shared by every thread.

### What the Swift wrapper owes you
- Mark it `@MainActor`. Exported Kotlin classes are Objective-C classes and are not `Sendable`, so Swift 6 strict concurrency will not let you carry them across isolation domains otherwise.
- Start the collection from `.task { }` so view teardown cancels the Swift task, and cancel the Kotlin handle in `deinit`.

Model: the compiler no longer protects you and the platform still does not forgive you — choose the thread deliberately, at exactly one place per stream.

Treat the exported surface as a designed product with exactly one consumer, not as whatever happened to be `public` in `commonMain` — because that is precisely what the header generator ships.

### Decide what leaves the module
- `internal` for everything the iOS app does not call. Repositories, use cases, DI wiring and mappers have no business in the header; they inflate it, the binary and the compile time.
- `@HiddenFromObjC`, under `@OptIn(ExperimentalObjCRefinement::class)`, drops a declaration that must stay `public` for Android out of the iOS header.
- `@ObjCName(swiftName = "…")` fixes a name that reads badly in Swift, and `@ShouldRefineInSwift` renames a declaration to `__name` so a Swift extension can wrap it in something idiomatic — the trick SKIE uses for flows and suspend functions.

### Shape what does leave
- One state type per screen, one stream of it, one function per user intent. Parameters and returns stay simple: `String`, `Int`, `Boolean`, lists, and your own exported data classes.
- Keep generics, `Result<T>`, deep sealed hierarchies and raw `Flow` out of the signature — Objective-C erases or hides all of them, and Swift is left with `Any` and switches it cannot make exhaustive.
- Errors belong in the state as a value, not as an exception thrown across the bridge.

### Let Swift finish the job
- Exported Kotlin classes are Objective-C classes, so a Swift extension in the app module can make them `Identifiable`, `Hashable` or `CustomStringConvertible` without touching Kotlin.
- Map Kotlin enums to Swift enums once, at the edge, so the rest of the app switches exhaustively — or let SKIE generate that layer.

Rule of thumb: if you would not put it in a REST response designed for this one app, do not put it in the header.

Swift export makes the Kotlin/Native compiler emit Swift bindings directly, so the API no longer has to be expressible in Objective-C first — which is where most of today's interop pain comes from.

### What it changes
- Kotlin classes stop being `NSObject` subclasses carrying a framework-name prefix. `SharedFeedViewModel` becomes `FeedViewModel` inside a real Swift module you `import`, with package structure you can collapse via `flattenPackage`.
- No `KotlinInt` or `NSNumber` boxing for nullable primitives, no mangled names for overloads, no implicitly unwrapped optionals standing in for non-null Kotlin types.
- The build wires up differently: a `swiftExport { }` block in the Gradle DSL and an `embedSwiftExportForXcode` task instead of `embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode`.

### What it still cannot do
- Suspend functions and `Flow` are not exported, which is most of the reason anyone reached for SKIE or KMP-NativeCoroutines in the first place.
- Generics support is partial and only a subset of the type system maps so far, so an API that survives the ObjC exporter may simply not come through.
- SKIE post-processes an Objective-C framework, so it does not apply here. Turning Swift export on means giving that up until the compiler covers the same ground.

### Shipping
- Prototype it now on a spare target; do not put a release on it while your ViewModels expose flows and suspend functions.
- The cheap insurance is API shape, not tooling. A narrow facade of value types with one state stream and one function per intent migrates almost for free; an API built around Objective-C tricks does not.

Mental model: Swift export replaces the Objective-C bridge rather than wrapping it, so whatever it does not cover yet is simply not there.
